top_choice_rationale: The magic-wavelength optical lattice clock is a specific, independently reproduced invention (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, PTB, NIST, SYRTE) whose 10^-18 systematic budgets are verified by clock-to-clock comparisons, and which has delivered measured new facts (millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, tighter bounds on drifting constants and dark-matter couplings, controlled many-body effects). The two-name allocation to Katori and Ye is clean and each name is essential. The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is a real reservation but can be handled by a citation that names the magic-wavelength lattice. The topological insulator trio (P002) is a strong and mature concept, but the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang and 3D omissions leave the credit weaker, so I rank it second ahead of no award.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile; Kroll works in atomic, molecular and optical physics at Lund, but has no stated connection to Katori or Ye (he spent a year in John Hall's lab as a PhD student, which is a distant link to the 2005 laureate's precision-spectroscopy lineage, not to the proposed laureates)
